options: She should cook the saleeg very quickly
She should stir slowly and take her time
She should cook early in the morning

questions.q: What can we understand from Grandma's words at the end of the story?
options: Cooking for people you love is part of what makes food special
Expensive ingredients are the most important thing in cooking
Only grandmothers can cook saleeg well

pages.text: It was the first week of the summer holidays, and Faisal's mother had asked him to help clear out the dusty storeroom on the roof. Behind a pile of old carpets, he noticed a strange wooden case covered in dust. When he opened it, he found an oud with a long crack across its body and two strings missing. He carried it downstairs carefully, as if it were made of glass.

"Where did you find that?" his grandfather asked, and his eyes suddenly looked younger. He explained that he had played this oud at family weddings in Taif for nearly forty years. "Then my hands began to shake, and I couldn't play properly anymore," he said quietly. "So I put it away, because it hurt too much to look at it." Faisal had never known that his grandfather was a musician.

The next morning, Faisal took the oud to Uncle Hamza, an old instrument maker who had a tiny shop in the souq. Uncle Hamza turned it over slowly and whistled. "This is excellent wood, but repairing it won't be cheap or quick," he warned. Faisal emptied his savings box onto the counter, money he had been keeping for a new phone, and said, "Please, I'll wait as long as it takes."

Three weeks later, the oud was as good as new, and Grandfather became Faisal's teacher. Although he couldn't play himself, he hummed each melody and told Faisal exactly where to put his fingers. At first, Faisal's fingertips were so sore that he wanted to give up. "Pain is the price of every beautiful sound," his grandfather said with a smile, so Faisal kept practising every evening after dinner.

In September, the school announced a Heritage Evening, and students were invited to share something from Saudi culture. Faisal signed up before he could change his mind. His cousin Nawaf laughed and said, "An oud? Nobody our age is interested in that old-fashioned stuff." That night, Faisal couldn't sleep because he had butterflies in his stomach, but he decided he wouldn't let Nawaf's words stop him.

On the evening of the show, the hall was full of parents, teachers and students, and Grandfather was sitting in the front row. Faisal walked onto the stage, sat down and began the old Taif melody his grandfather loved. Everything was going perfectly until, halfway through the song, there was a sharp sound. One of the strings had broken, and the hall went completely silent.

Faisal's face burned, and for a moment he wanted to run off the stage. Then he looked down at the front row, where his grandfather had started clapping a slow, steady rhythm. Soon the parents around him joined in, and then the whole hall was clapping together. Taking a deep breath, Faisal found new places for his fingers and continued the melody on just five strings.

When the last note faded, the audience jumped to their feet and cheered, and even Nawaf was clapping the loudest. Afterwards, Grandfather held Faisal's hands in his own shaking ones. "Tonight you didn't just play music," he said. "You gave my oud its voice back, and you gave me mine too." Faisal realised that some things are worth far more than a new phone.

questions.q: Why did Grandfather stop playing the oud?
What did Faisal give up to pay for the repair?
options: Money he was saving for a new phone

questions.q: In the story, what does 'sore' mean?
What happened in the middle of Faisal's performance?
Why did Grandfather say Faisal had given him his voice back?
options: Faisal had taught him to sing
Faisal had bought him a new oud
Through Faisal, his music could be heard again

stories.title: The Watch That Should Not Tick

pages.text: Faris spent every Saturday at his grandfather's watch shop in the old part of Jeddah. The shop was small and dusty and full of ticking clocks, and he loved it more than any shopping mall. In the window sat Grandfather's most precious possession: a silver pocket watch that had belonged to his own grandfather. Its hands always pointed to quarter to four, because nobody had wound it for sixty years. "Some things are more beautiful when they rest," Grandfather liked to say.

That Saturday, a well-dressed man in a grey thobe came in and asked to see the silver watch. He held it for a long time, turning it over in his hands and taking photos of it with his phone. "I'll pay you twenty thousand riyals for it," he offered. Grandfather smiled politely and shook his head. "I'm sorry, but it isn't for sale at any price."

The next morning, Faris arrived early to help Yousef, the young apprentice, open the shop. As he walked past the window, he stopped suddenly. The silver watch looked exactly the same as always, but something felt wrong. He bent closer and heard a soft, steady sound: tick, tick, tick.

"Grandfather, your watch is working!" Faris called. Grandfather hurried over, picked it up and frowned. "This isn't my watch," he said quietly. "It's a very good copy, but whoever made it forgot one important detail." Yousef went pale, because he was the only other person with a key to the shop.

Grandfather looked worried, but Faris refused to believe that Yousef was guilty. He remembered the man in the grey thobe and all the photos he had taken. "Someone needed those photos to make a copy," he said slowly. "But they still had to get close enough to swap the watches." He looked around the shop carefully, just like the detectives in his favourite books.

Faris asked Yousef whether anyone had come in after Grandfather left for the Maghrib prayer the evening before. Yousef thought for a moment. "The man in the grey thobe came back," he admitted. "He wanted one last look at the watch, so I gave it to him while I answered the phone." Faris and Grandfather looked at each other, then up at the small camera above the door.

On the video, they watched the man take something from his pocket and swap the two watches in less than three seconds. Grandfather phoned the police straight away, and they found the man before the end of the day. He had been planning to sell the real watch to a collector abroad. By evening, the silver watch was back in Grandfather's hands, still showing quarter to four.

That night, Yousef apologised again and again for his mistake. "You were tricked by a clever thief," Grandfather said kindly. "The important thing is that you told the truth." Then he turned to Faris with a proud smile. "A clock that ticks can be useful, but a detective who listens is priceless."

questions.q: Why did the silver watch always show quarter to four?
options: Because nobody had wound it for sixty years
Because it was broken by a customer
Because Grandfather set it every morning

questions.q: How did Faris know that the watch in the window was not the real one?
options: It had a crack in the glass

questions.q: In the story, what does "apprentice" mean?
options: A young person learning a job from an expert

questions.q: Why did Yousef go pale when Grandfather said the watch was a copy?
options: He was afraid people would think he stole it
He had broken the real watch

questions.q: What does Grandfather mean when he says "a detective who listens is priceless"?
options: Faris's careful attention to small things is very valuable

pages.text: Yousef discovered his strange power on the most boring afternoon of his life. He was sitting at the back of the classroom while his teacher talked about rocks, and nobody was looking at him. Suddenly, he glanced down and saw that his hands had disappeared. He could still feel his fingers, but he couldn't see them at all.

After a week of secret experiments in his bedroom, Yousef understood the rules. He became invisible only when nobody in the world was thinking about him. The moment someone remembered him, like his mother calling him for dinner or his little sister Noura looking for her charger, he appeared again. "It's not exactly a superpower," he complained to his grandfather, the only person he had told. "It's a superpower for people nobody notices."

Grandfather put down his cup of tea and smiled. "Every power has a purpose, Yousef. Perhaps yours is waiting for the right moment." Yousef wasn't convinced. Heroes in films could fly or lift cars, but he could only vanish when he felt forgotten.

The right moment came on a busy Thursday evening at a shopping mall in Jeddah. Yousef's family was buying shoes when the lights went out and an alarm began to scream. Smoke was pouring from a kitchen near the food court, and hundreds of people rushed towards the exits in panic. In the confusion, Yousef heard a small voice crying behind a storeroom door.

A security guard was shouting into his radio, and nobody was paying attention to a quiet fourteen-year-old. Yousef felt the familiar tingle and watched his body fade into nothing. He slipped through a gap in a barrier that the guards would never have let him pass. Inside the storeroom, a boy of about six was hiding under a shelf, coughing and terrified.

"I can't see you!" the boy whispered when Yousef spoke to him. "That's fine. Just hold my hand and keep your head down," Yousef said calmly, although his own heart was racing. Together they crawled along the floor, where the air was cleaner, until they reached an emergency exit that was blocked by boxes. Yousef pushed the boxes aside one by one and led the boy out into the cool night air.

The boy's father ran forward and hugged his son, looking around in surprise for the person who had helped him. Then Yousef heard his mother's voice calling his name desperately. At that moment his whole family was thinking about him, and he reappeared, covered in dust. His mother held him tightly, Noura burst into tears, and his father kept saying "Alhamdulillah" again and again.

Later that night, Grandfather sat beside Yousef on the balcony. "So, is it still a useless power?" he asked with a twinkle in his eye. Yousef laughed and shook his head. He had learned something important that evening. Being invisible had helped him save someone, but becoming visible again because people loved him felt even better.

questions.q: When does Yousef become invisible?
options: When nobody is thinking about him

What does the word "vanish" mean in the story?
Why did Yousef and the boy crawl along the floor?
options: Because they were playing a game
Because the air near the floor was cleaner
Because the guards were chasing them

questions.q: What is the main message of the ending?
options: Being loved by your family matters more than being special
It is better to stay invisible forever

pages.text: Faris had been counting the days until the camping trip to the Nafud desert. On Thursday afternoon, his father and Uncle Saad loaded the car with a tent, blankets, a gas cooker and enough water for three days. His cousin Nawaf, who was only eleven, had brought something special: a small drone with a camera. "I'm going to film the best sunset in Saudi Arabia," he announced proudly.

By the time they had set up the tent among the red dunes, the sun was already low. Father lit a fire and made cardamom coffee while Uncle Saad cooked chicken kabsa in a big pot. Nawaf sent his drone high into the golden sky, and the boys watched the screen in amazement. Then a strong wind suddenly blew from the north, and the drone disappeared behind a tall dune.

"My birthday present!" Nawaf cried. "Don't worry, it can't be far," Faris said. Without telling the adults, the two boys ran after the signal on the controller. They climbed one dune, then another, and soon they had completely lost track of time.

They finally found the drone lying in the soft sand, its battery almost empty. Faris turned around to lead the way back, but his heart sank. Every dune looked exactly the same in the fading light, and the wind had already erased their footprints. Even worse, his phone had no signal, and Nawaf's controller had just died.

Nawaf's voice began to shake. "We're lost, aren't we?" Faris felt afraid too, but he knew that panicking would only make things worse. He closed his eyes and remembered his grandfather's words on the roof of their house in Hail: "When the sand lies to you, the sky will tell you the truth."

As darkness covered the desert, the stars appeared one by one. Faris searched the sky until he found the seven bright stars his grandfather called Banat Na'sh, and they led his eyes to a small, steady star: Al-Jadi, the North Star. "The wind came from the north, so it blew the drone south," he explained. "That means our camp is north of us. We just have to walk towards that star."

They walked slowly, holding hands and keeping the star in front of them. After about twenty minutes, Nawaf pointed and shouted. Far away, a small orange light was flickering at the bottom of a dune: the campfire! They could also hear Uncle Saad's voice calling their names across the sand.

Father hugged them both tightly, then gave them a long, serious look. "You should never have left without telling us," he said, "but I'm proud that you kept a cool head." Later that night, Faris called his grandfather, who laughed warmly when he heard the whole story. "The sky has guided our people for a thousand years," the old man said, "and now it's your turn to teach Nawaf."

options: To collect wood for the fire
To watch the sunset from a higher dune

questions.q: Who taught Faris about the stars?
In the story, the campfire was "flickering". What does this mean?
options: It was burning very fast and hot
Its light was moving and shining unsteadily

questions.q: How did Faris know that the camp was to the north?
options: He saw tire tracks going north
The wind had blown the drone south from the camp
His phone showed him the direction

questions.q: How did Father feel when the boys returned?
options: Only angry, because they broke the drone
Worried about their mistake, but proud of how Faris acted
Surprised that they had been away at all

stories.title: The Notebook in the Lost-and-Found Box

pages.text: Every Monday, Yousef stayed after the last bell to empty the school's lost-and-found box. Most weeks it held the usual things: odd socks from PE, a broken ruler, someone's forgotten water bottle. But this Monday, under a pile of jackets, he found something he had never seen before. It was a small notebook with a faded blue cover and no name on it.

He opened it, expecting someone's maths homework. Instead, every page was covered with pencil drawings of the school: the main gate, the science lab, the old palm tree by the car park. They were so detailed that Yousef could almost hear the noise of the playground. "Whoever drew these is seriously talented," he whispered.

The next morning he showed the notebook to his best friend, Hamad. "Just put a notice on the board," Hamad suggested. "The owner will come for it." But three days passed, and nobody came. "Finding the artist in a school of six hundred students is like looking for a needle in a haystack," Hamad sighed.

Yousef refused to give up. That evening he studied the drawings more carefully and noticed something strange. In one picture, the library had a wooden door, but that door had been replaced with a glass one years ago. In another, the palm tree was only as tall as a man, although now it reached the roof.

"These weren't drawn recently," Yousef told Hamad at break. "Some of them must be twenty or thirty years old." Hamad's eyes widened. "So the owner isn't a student at all?" Together they made a list of everyone who had worked at the school for a long time, and only one name had been there longer than the palm tree: Uncle Saleh, the caretaker.

They found him in the small workshop behind the gym, fixing a broken chair. When Yousef held up the notebook, the old man's face lit up. "I thought I'd lost this forever!" he exclaimed. He explained that he had drawn the school every year since he arrived, and that he was retiring at the end of the month. "I wanted to take my memories with me," he said quietly.

Walking home, Yousef couldn't stop thinking about what he had heard. Uncle Saleh had looked after the school for thirty-two years, yet most students didn't even know his name. "We should do something for him," he told Hamad, who grinned and agreed immediately. With the headteacher's permission, they spent two weeks secretly scanning the drawings and preparing a surprise.

On Uncle Saleh's last day, he was asked to come to the school hall. When the doors opened, he saw his drawings printed in large frames along the walls, and hundreds of students clapping. Beside each picture, a student had written a thank-you note. The old man wiped his eyes and turned to Yousef. "You returned more than a notebook, my son," he said. "You gave me back thirty-two years."

options: Stopping work because of age or a long career

pages.text: Lina had always thought her grandmother's storeroom was full of nothing but dust and old carpets. But that Friday afternoon, the family was preparing for Grandma Noura to move into their house in Jeddah, and Lina found a small wooden box hidden behind a pile of blankets. Inside was a cassette tape with faded handwriting on the label: "For Noura – 1979." Lina's heart began to beat faster.

"That's Grandpa's writing," said her older brother, Omar, looking over her shoulder. Their grandfather had died before Lina was born, and she knew him only from photographs and the stories her father told at dinner. "We have to play it," she whispered. The problem was that nobody in the family had owned a cassette player for at least twenty years.

After searching the whole house, they finally discovered an ancient player in a cupboard in their father's study. Omar pressed the button, but nothing happened except a sad clicking sound. "It's broken," he sighed. "Maybe we should just forget about it." Lina refused to give up so easily, and she remembered a tiny electronics shop in Al-Balad, the old part of the city, where her father used to get his watch repaired.

The next evening, their father drove them through the narrow streets, past the tall coral-stone houses with their wooden balconies. The shop owner, an elderly man called Abu Saleh, examined the machine through thick glasses. "The belt inside has worn out," he explained, "but I think I still have one somewhere." While he worked, he told them that people used to send recorded messages to their families when phone calls abroad were too expensive.

When they got home, Lina and Omar shut themselves in her bedroom and pressed play. At first there was only a soft hiss, and then a young man's voice filled the room, warm and slightly nervous. "Assalamu alaikum, Noura. It's snowing here in Colorado, and I have never been so cold in my life!" Lina and Omar stared at each other in amazement, because the voice sounded almost exactly like their father's.

On the tape, Grandpa described his engineering classes, his kind neighbours and his terrible first attempt at cooking kabsa alone. He laughed at himself so much that Omar couldn't stop laughing too. Near the end, his voice became quieter. "I've started writing a poem for you, but I'll only finish it when I'm home again," he said, and he recited the first lines. Then the tape suddenly stopped.

"He never finished it," Lina said sadly. Omar frowned. "Or maybe he did, but not on tape." They decided to keep their secret until Grandma Noura had settled into her new room. On her first evening with them, after the family had eaten dinner together, Lina placed the old player on the table and asked everyone to listen.

As soon as she heard the voice, Grandma Noura put her hand over her mouth, and her eyes filled with tears. Their father sat completely still, as if he were listening to a stranger he had always known. When the tape reached the unfinished poem, Grandma closed her eyes and, in a soft, steady voice, recited the final lines that Grandpa had written for her more than forty years ago. Nobody spoke for a long moment, and then Grandma smiled at Lina and said, "Thank you for bringing him home."

pages.text: Faisal's grandfather, Abu Saleh, had grown dates in Al-Ahsa for fifty years, and he didn't trust anything with a screen. "A palm tree speaks to the man who listens," he liked to say. So when Faisal arrived for the summer holidays with a box of tiny sensors and a tablet, his grandfather raised an eyebrow. "What are those? Toys?"

"They're soil sensors, Grandpa," Faisal explained. "If the ground gets too dry, they send a message to my phone." He had built them himself for a school science competition, using a cheap kit and a lot of online videos. His grandfather laughed kindly, but he agreed to let Faisal put them under five of the oldest palms.

For the first week, nothing interesting happened. Every morning, the screen showed five green circles, which meant the soil was healthy. Faisal's cousin Noura, who was visiting with her family, teased him about it. "Your invention is very good at saying 'everything is fine'," she said with a grin.

Then, at three o'clock one night, Faisal's phone buzzed loudly. One circle had turned red: Tree 4 – soil dry. He frowned, confused, because the water pump had been running for hours. Something didn't add up, so he grabbed a torch and went to wake his grandfather.

At first, Abu Saleh was annoyed, but he got up anyway. Out on the dark farm, the air was hot and heavy, and they could hear the pump humming steadily. Faisal pointed his torch at Tree 4. The ground around it was cracked and dusty, even though water should have been flowing there.

His grandfather knelt down and pressed his hand against the earth, then walked slowly along the line of the old pipe. About twenty metres away, he stopped. "Listen," he whispered. Under the sand, they heard a faint sound of rushing water – the pipe had broken, and the water was disappearing deep underground instead of reaching the trees.

By sunrise, they had dug up the broken piece and replaced it with help from Faisal's uncle. "In this heat, the trees would have suffered for days before I noticed," Abu Saleh admitted, wiping his forehead. "Your little machine heard the problem, but it took an old man's ears to find it." Faisal smiled, because he realised they had both been right.

Before the holiday ended, his grandfather asked for ten more sensors – one for every row of palms. He even gave Tree 4 a nickname: "the Messenger". Back at school, Faisal won second prize in the competition, but his favourite moment wasn't on the stage. It was a voice message from Grandpa that said, "Green circles today. The Messenger says hello."

stories.title: The Madman Who Caught the Light

pages.text: In the busy city of Cairo, in the year 1015, a thirteen-year-old boy named Yusuf had an unusual job. Every morning, he carried bread and dates to a quiet house near the great mosque of Al-Azhar. Two guards always stood outside the door, and the neighbours whispered that a madman lived inside. Yusuf's hands shook the first time he knocked, because he had no idea what was waiting for him.

The room was dark, but the man sitting in it did not look mad at all. He was writing calmly by the light of a small lamp, and he smiled when he saw the frightened boy. "People say you've lost your mind," Yusuf said nervously, before he could stop himself. The man laughed softly. "People say many things, my young friend. My name is Al-Hasan Ibn al-Haytham, and I am as sane as you are."

Over the following weeks, the scholar told Yusuf his secret. Years earlier, he had boasted to the powerful ruler of Egypt that he could control the floods of the River Nile. However, when he travelled south and saw the mighty river with his own eyes, he realised the task was impossible. Instead of facing the ruler's anger, he had pretended to be mad, and so he had been locked in this house. "Sometimes a wise man must look foolish in order to survive," he explained.

One bright afternoon, Yusuf noticed something strange on the wall opposite the window. A tiny hole in the wooden shutter was letting in a thin beam of sunlight, and on the wall there was a picture of the street outside. He could see camels, a fruit seller and a palm tree, but everything was upside down! "Is it magic?" Yusuf gasped, and Ibn al-Haytham's eyes shone with excitement.

"It isn't magic, it's light," the scholar replied. "For centuries, famous thinkers believed that our eyes send out rays to see things, but I'm convinced they were wrong. Light travels from objects into our eyes, and it always moves in straight lines." Then he gave Yusuf advice that the boy never forgot. "Don't believe something just because a famous man wrote it in a book. Test it yourself."

From that day on, Yusuf became his helper rather than just a delivery boy. Together they made holes of different sizes, moved lamps around the room and carefully measured every shadow. Whenever an experiment failed, Ibn al-Haytham simply wrote down the result and tried again. Slowly, the pile of pages on his desk grew taller, and Yusuf grew taller too.

Six years passed before surprising news spread through Cairo: the ruler had mysteriously disappeared. The guards left their posts, and for the first time in years, Ibn al-Haytham stepped out into the sunshine. Under his arm he carried a thick bundle of pages, which he called the Book of Optics. "My prison was the best laboratory I could have wished for," he told Yusuf with a grin.

Years later, the Book of Optics was translated into many languages, and scientists all over the world studied it for centuries. Its ideas about light, the eye and careful experiments helped to shape modern science and, much later, the invention of the camera. Yusuf grew up to become a respected teacher in Cairo. Whenever a student asked him a difficult question, he would smile and say, "Don't just believe me. Test it yourself."

pages.text: Faisal had kept a weather diary since he was ten. Every morning before school, he checked the temperature, the wind and the clouds outside his home in Taif, and he wrote everything down in a blue notebook. His sister Noura called him "the weather detective," and she didn't always mean it kindly. But Faisal didn't mind, because he believed the sky was always trying to tell people something.

One Friday in spring, the family drove out to a wide, dry valley for a picnic with their grandfather. The sky above them was perfectly blue, and the sand was warm under their feet. Grandfather spread out the carpet near a group of acacia trees in the middle of the valley, and Mother began pouring cups of tea. "Not a single cloud," said Father happily. "We picked the perfect day."

Faisal, however, kept looking towards the mountains in the west. Dark grey clouds were piling up behind the peaks, and every few minutes he saw a tiny flash of light. He checked the weather app on his father's phone, but there was no signal out here. "Those clouds are too far away to worry about," Noura said, biting into a date. "You're not going to get wet, detective."

Faisal wasn't so sure. In science class, Mr. Saeed had explained that heavy rain in the mountains could rush down into a dry valley many kilometres away, even when the sky above it was clear. "That's called a flash flood," he had said, "and it can arrive in minutes." Faisal noticed that the ground beneath the acacia trees was smooth and covered in small stones, as if water had passed through here before. His heart began to beat faster.

"Grandfather," he said quietly, pointing at the clouds and the stones, "I think we're sitting in the path of the water." Father laughed and said they had only just arrived, but Grandfather didn't laugh. He stood up slowly, sniffed the wind and studied the sand. "When I was a boy, my father taught me never to trust a dry wadi," he said. "Pack everything. We're moving to higher ground."

Noura complained all the way up the rocky slope, carrying the flask and a bag of oranges. They set up the carpet again on a flat hill above the valley, and Mother poured the tea for the second time. For a while nothing happened, and Faisal started to feel embarrassed. Then he heard it: a low, deep roar, like a huge truck coming closer.

A wall of brown water came racing around the bend in the valley, carrying branches, mud and stones. Within seconds it had covered the place where they had been sitting, and the acacia trees were standing in a fast, angry river. Noura grabbed her brother's arm, her eyes wide. Nobody said a word as they watched the water rush past below them, while the sun still shone brightly overhead.

An hour later, the flood had become a gentle stream, and the valley smelled of wet earth. Grandfather put his hand on Faisal's shoulder and smiled. "You read the sky like a scientist, and I read it like my father did," he said. "Today we both told the same story." On the drive home, Noura borrowed the blue notebook and, in her neatest handwriting, wrote: Never trust a dry wadi. — Noura, assistant weather detective.

stories.title: The Stars on the Old Wall

pages.text: Every Friday, Faris helped his grandfather at his small perfume shop in Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. He loved the narrow streets, the tall coral-stone houses and the wooden balconies that hung over the lanes like old lanterns. One morning, on his way to the shop, he noticed something strange on a crumbling wall: a small eight-pointed star, painted in deep blue and gold. The paint was still wet.

The next Friday there were two stars, and the week after that, five, joined together by thin white lines. "Someone is painting at night," Faris told his older sister, Lama, who was studying design at university. She looked at the photos on his phone and frowned. "This isn't graffiti," she said slowly. "These are traditional patterns, and whoever made them really knows what they're doing."

Faris couldn't stop thinking about the mystery. He started copying the stars into his sketchbook, trying to work out how the lines fitted together, but every pattern seemed more complicated than the last. His grandfather smiled when he saw the drawings. "Patterns like these used to be everywhere in Al-Balad," he said. "Doors, windows, ceilings... but most of the people who could make them have passed away."

Determined to solve the mystery, Faris and Lama decided to walk to the wall straight after the dawn prayer one Friday. The street was quiet and grey, and a cool wind was blowing from the sea. As they turned the corner, they saw an old man sitting on a low stool, holding a brush in a shaking hand. It was Uncle Saleh, the carpenter whose workshop had been closed for years.

Uncle Saleh looked embarrassed, as if he had been caught doing something wrong. "When I was young, I carved and painted half the doors in this street," he explained quietly. "Now my eyes are getting weaker, and I'm afraid that one day I'll forget the patterns completely." "So I paint them here, where I can see them every morning." Faris opened his sketchbook and showed him his copies, and the old man's face lit up.

From that day on, the three of them met every Friday morning. Uncle Saleh explained how each pattern was built from a single circle, while Faris drew carefully and Lama measured every angle and photographed the finished stars. Little by little, the empty wall turned into a garden of blue, gold and white shapes. Neighbours began stopping to watch, and some even brought tea and dates.

One morning, a woman from the city's heritage office arrived with a notebook. She had seen Lama's photos online, and she wanted to know who was responsible for the wall. "These designs could have been lost forever," she said. "Would you agree to teach them to young people, Uncle Saleh?" The old man looked at Faris and Lama for a long moment before he answered.

"Only if these two help me," he said with a smile. Two months later, the first class took place in his old workshop, which had been cleaned and repainted for the occasion. Faris stood at the front beside Uncle Saleh, showing twenty students how to draw a perfect circle. Outside, on the old coral wall, a new star was drying in the sun, and this time Faris had painted it himself.

pages.text: Faisal had imagined a summer of football and video games, but instead he was spending it in an old coral-stone house in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. His grandfather had bought the house years ago, and now they were restoring it together, room by room. There was dust everywhere, the heat was terrible, and his phone had no signal. "Just don't open the green window on the top floor," his grandfather said on the first morning. "Not yet."

For three days, Faisal tried to forget about the window, but he simply couldn't. It was a beautiful wooden roshan, painted the colour of young palm leaves, with tiny holes that let the sea breeze in. On the fourth afternoon, while his grandfather was resting, Faisal climbed the narrow stairs and pushed it open. Immediately, the noise of the traffic disappeared, and the air smelled of salt, bread and spices.

Below him, the street had completely changed. There were no cars, only men pulling wooden carts and sellers shouting about fresh fish and dates. Faisal ran downstairs and was amazed to find that the house was no longer dusty and broken but brand new. He stepped outside, his heart beating fast, and realised that he was standing in the Jeddah of seventy years ago.

Near the door, a boy of about his age was searching the ground desperately. "I've lost the key to my father's shop," the boy explained, wiping his eyes. "He's coming back from Makkah tonight, and if the shop isn't open, he'll be so disappointed in me." Faisal introduced himself, and the boy said his name was Ibrahim. "Don't worry," Faisal said. "Let's think about where you've been today."

Together they followed Ibrahim's path through the busy market, checking every corner and asking every seller. At last, Faisal noticed something shining under the wheel of a cart that had been parked outside the bakery. It was the key! Ibrahim laughed with relief and gave Faisal a handful of sweet dates. "Where are you from?" he asked, staring at Faisal's digital watch. "Not far away," Faisal replied with a smile.

Just then, the call to the sunset prayer rose over the rooftops, and Faisal realised that he had completely lost track of time. He said a quick goodbye, raced back into the house and climbed the stairs two at a time. As soon as he closed the green window, the sound of car horns returned. His phone buzzed in his pocket, and the house was dusty and old once again.

His grandfather was waiting at the bottom of the stairs, but he didn't look angry at all. Instead, his eyes were shining. "You found my key, didn't you?" he asked quietly. Faisal stared at him, unable to speak. Slowly, the old man took a small brass key from his pocket, the same key that Faisal had held only a few minutes earlier.

"I've been waiting seventy years to thank you properly," said his grandfather, whose name, of course, was Ibrahim. "When you were born, I recognised your face at once, and that's why I bought this house." That night, Faisal didn't touch his phone; he listened to his grandfather's stories until very late. Before he went to sleep, he climbed upstairs and gently checked that the green window was closed. "Not yet," he whispered, smiling.

pages.text: Every Saturday morning, Faris went with his grandfather to the quiet lagoon near their town on the Red Sea coast. Grandfather had fished there for nearly fifty years, and he knew every tree and every bird by heart. But this Saturday, something was wrong. The water smelled strange, and the leaves of the mangrove trees were turning yellow.

"Where are the herons?" Faris asked, looking up at the empty branches. Grandfather shook his head slowly. "When I was young, the sea came in and went out twice a day, as if it were breathing," he said. Faris looked down at the water and noticed that it wasn't moving at all.

That evening, Faris told his cousin Noura, who was in the science club at her school. Noura had been learning to fly a small drone, and her eyes lit up. "Let's look at the lagoon from above," she suggested. The next day, the drone's camera showed something they had never noticed before: a new road, and a huge pile of rocks and sand blocking the narrow channel that connected the lagoon to the sea.

Faris and Noura walked to the building site with Grandfather to ask about it. An engineer in a white helmet listened politely, then shrugged. "It's only a small stream," he said. "It doesn't really matter." On the way home, Faris kicked a stone angrily and said, "Nobody cares about a few trees."

"Getting angry won't help," Noura said firmly. "We need evidence, not just feelings." For two weeks, they measured the water, counted the birds and took photos of the dying leaves. Grandfather even found an old album with pictures from 1985, which showed the lagoon full of fish and white herons.

Their school principal was so impressed by their project that she arranged for them to present it at a meeting at the municipality. On the day of the meeting, Faris's hands were shaking and his mouth felt dry. He glanced at Grandfather, who was sitting in the front row and nodded calmly. Faris took a deep breath and began to speak.

When the official watched the drone video and saw the old photos next to the new ones, he was silent for a long moment. "I honestly had no idea," he admitted. "Without that channel, the whole lagoon could die." He promised that large pipes would be put under the road so the sea water could flow freely again.

A month later, workers removed the rocks and laid the pipes, and the water began to rush back into the lagoon. By the end of the year, the mangrove leaves were green again, and one bright morning, the herons returned. Grandfather smiled and put his hand on Faris's shoulder. "Listen," he whispered. "The sea is breathing again."

pages.text: Reem had spent four months building Sahm, a small robot that could find its way through a maze in under a minute. Tomorrow, she would take it to the regional robotics competition in Riyadh. Before bed, her grandfather placed a tiny box in her hand. "A spare motor," he said with a smile. "In my experience, things always break at the worst possible moment."

The only other girl from her school in the competition was Hala, who had joined their class in September. Hala rarely spoke to anyone, and when Reem had once offered to show her the library, she had simply said, "I'm fine, thanks," and walked away. Since then, most girls had decided she was unfriendly. Reem wasn't so sure, because sometimes Hala looked less proud than lonely.

The competition hall was huge and noisy, full of nervous teams and excited parents. Reem's first run went perfectly, and Sahm finished the maze in forty-eight seconds. Then it was Hala's turn. Her robot rolled forward confidently, turned left, and suddenly stopped as a thin line of smoke rose from its wheel.

The judges gave Hala fifteen minutes to repair it before the final run. Reem watched her open the robot with shaking hands. "The motor's burnt out," Hala whispered to nobody in particular. "I can't fix this. It's over." She looked as if she was trying very hard not to cry in front of hundreds of people.

Reem felt the small box in her pocket. If she gave Hala the motor, she would have nothing left if Sahm broke too, and Hala's robot was fast, perhaps faster than hers. A voice in her head said, "It's not your problem." But another voice, which sounded a lot like her grandfather's, asked, "What would you want someone to do for you?"

She walked over and held out the box. "I think it's the same size as yours," she said. Hala stared at her, confused. "Why would you help me? We're competing against each other." Reem shrugged and replied, "Because winning against a broken robot isn't really winning," and together they fitted the motor with less than a minute to spare.

In the final, Hala's robot finished in forty-five seconds, three seconds faster than Sahm. Reem came second, and for a moment she felt a sharp sting of disappointment. Then Hala ran across the hall and hugged her tightly. "I've moved schools three times in two years," she said quietly. "I stopped trying to make friends because I always had to leave them, but I'm staying this time, and I'd really like to have one."

That evening, Reem told her grandfather everything, expecting him to be a little sad about the silver medal. Instead, he laughed. "So something did break at the worst possible moment," he said, "just not in your robot." A month later, the school announced that Reem and Hala would represent Riyadh together at the national finals, and they both agreed immediately on a name for their new robot: Sadeeq, which means "friend".

pages.text: Faisal had been looking forward to this trip for months. Every spring, his grandfather took the family camping in Wadi Disah, a deep valley in the north of Saudi Arabia where palm trees grow between tall red cliffs. This year, Faisal's cousin Omar had come too, and Faisal had brought his new drone. 'Remember one thing,' Grandfather said as they put up the tents. 'The wadi remembers the water, even when the sky forgets.'

The next morning, the boys asked for permission to walk to the narrow part of the canyon, where ancient carvings of camels covered the rocks. Grandfather looked up at the clear blue sky and nodded. 'Be back before Dhuhr prayer,' he said. 'And keep your eyes on the mountains, not just on your screen.'

The carvings were even more amazing than Faisal had imagined. While Omar took photos, Faisal sent the drone high above the cliffs to film the canyon from the air. On the small screen, he noticed something strange: far away, over the mountains, a wall of dark grey cloud was growing. Above the boys, however, the sun was still shining brightly.

At first, they laughed about it. 'It's miles away,' Omar said, shrugging. But then Faisal remembered his grandfather's words, and his smile disappeared. Rain in the mountains could rush down the dry valleys as a sudden flood, faster than a person could run. Then they heard it: a low rumbling sound, like a huge truck coming closer.

'Climb!' Faisal shouted, grabbing his drone. The boys scrambled up the rocks towards a wide ledge, scraping their hands and knees as they went. Seconds after they reached it, brown water came rushing round the corner, carrying branches and stones. The path they had been standing on only a minute before had completely disappeared.

They were safe, but they were trapped, and their phones had no signal. 'Grandfather will think we're lost,' Omar said, his voice shaking. Faisal looked at the drone in his hands, and suddenly an idea came to him. He tore a page from his notebook and wrote a message in big letters. Then he taped it carefully under the drone.

The drone's battery was low, so there was no time to waste. Faisal flew it back down the valley, following the line of palm trees towards the camp. On the screen, he saw tiny figures running out of the tents, all looking up at the sky. The message said: 'WE ARE SAFE ON A HIGH LEDGE NEAR THE CARVINGS. WE WILL WAIT.' A moment later, his grandfather raised both arms and waved.

Two hours later, when the water had gone down, Grandfather and Uncle Saleh arrived with ropes and bottles of water. They helped the boys climb down slowly, and Grandfather hugged them both tightly. 'You didn't panic, and you used your head,' he said. Then he smiled at Faisal. 'Today the wadi remembered the water, and you remembered my words.'

questions.q: Where did Faisal's family go camping?

pages.text: Noura had always believed that the Arabian leopard was more like a legend than a real animal. There were fewer than two hundred left in the wild, and most people had never seen one. So when her uncle Khalid, a wildlife ranger in AlUla, invited her and her younger brother Saad to spend the winter holiday with him, she packed her notebook before her clothes. "Don't get too excited," her uncle warned on the phone. "We've been searching for months, and we haven't found a single sign."

On their first morning, they drove into the mountains to check the camera traps. These small cameras were hidden among the rocks and took a photo whenever something moved in front of them. The first three cameras showed foxes, a few birds and one very surprised hare. But the fourth camera was lying on the ground, and its plastic case was scratched and cracked. "Someone must have knocked it over on purpose," Saad said angrily.

Noura wasn't so sure. She knelt down and studied the soft sand beside the rock. There, pressed into the ground, were round footprints, each with four toes and no claw marks. "Uncle, look," she whispered. "Dogs leave claw marks, but cats keep their claws in when they walk."

Uncle Khalid crouched beside her, and for a long moment he didn't say anything at all. "These prints are fresh," he said finally, his voice shaking slightly, "and they're far too big for a wildcat." He checked the memory card inside the broken camera while Saad measured the tracks with a ruler from Noura's bag. The last photo showed only a blur of golden fur and a long, spotted tail, but it was enough to make all three of them cheer.

Unfortunately, their excitement didn't last long. Dark clouds had been gathering over the mountains all afternoon, and suddenly the radio crackled with a flood warning. "When it rains here, the valley can fill with water in minutes," Uncle Khalid said. "We can't drive back now, so we'll have to wait it out." They climbed up to a shallow cave above the wadi and watched as heavy rain turned the dry valley into a roaring brown river.

The storm passed during the night, and Noura woke just before sunrise. The air smelled of wet stone, and everything was perfectly quiet. Then she noticed something moving on the rocks across the valley. A large cat with a pale golden coat was walking slowly along a ledge, and behind her, struggling to keep up, was a tiny cub.

Noura reached out and gently woke her uncle and brother. "Don't make a sound, and don't move," Uncle Khalid breathed. "She knows we're here, but we're too far away to worry her." For several minutes, they hardly dared to breathe as the mother leopard stopped to drink from a pool of rainwater. Then she looked straight across the valley at them, as if she were deciding whether they could be trusted, before disappearing among the rocks with her cub.

Back at the ranger station, Uncle Khalid reported the sighting to his team, and soon the news had spread across the whole country. A cub meant the leopards were not just surviving; they were having families again. "You found the tracks, Noura," her uncle said with a smile, "so you should choose the cub's name." She thought about the storm, the long months of searching and that brave little cub on the ledge. "Amal," she said, which means "hope".

pages.text: Six months ago, a small cube no bigger than a lunchbox left Earth on a rocket. Noura and her classmates had spent a whole year building it, and they named it Sadaa, which means "echo" in Arabic. For three weeks it sent back amazing photos of clouds over the Red Sea. Then, one morning, it went completely silent.

"I'm afraid it's gone," her teacher said gently. "Next week it will fall into the atmosphere and burn up like a shooting star." That evening, Noura told her grandfather, who had worked as a radio operator at the airport for forty years. He put down his cup of tea and smiled. "A satellite is never truly silent until it's gone," he said.

On Thursday night they drove out into the desert, far from the city lights. Grandfather unpacked an old radio and a homemade antenna made from metal measuring tapes. Above them, the sky was so clear that the Milky Way looked like spilled milk. "Sadaa will pass over us at 11:42," Noura said, checking the tracking app on her phone.

At 11:40 they switched the radio on. There was nothing but a soft hiss, like wind moving across the sand. Noura held the antenna high and slowly followed the satellite's path across the stars. Her arms began to ache, but she refused to give up.

Suddenly, a faint beeping came through the speaker. Grandfather's eyes lit up. "That's it! The battery must have recovered in the sunlight," he whispered. Noura's heart was beating so fast that she almost dropped the antenna.

Then the beeping stopped, and a voice began to speak. It was her own voice! Months earlier, each student had recorded a short message for the satellite's memory, and Noura had completely forgotten about hers. "Hello from Earth," the small voice said. "If anyone hears this, remember that we were curious, and we tried."

The signal faded as Sadaa disappeared over the horizon. Noura sat down on the cool sand, unable to speak. Grandfather pressed a button on his old recorder, which had captured every second. "Your classmates will want to hear this," he said softly.

On Sunday, the whole class listened in silence as the recording played, and some of the girls had tears in their eyes. Five days later, Noura and her grandfather watched a bright line of light cross the night sky and vanish. Sadaa had done exactly what its name promised: it had sent their voices back to them. And Noura was already sketching plans for the next one.
